newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan oil refinery hit by crude port shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan oil refinery hit by crude port shutdown.

text.p: In a new setback for Taiwan's giant oil monopoly, the shutdown of a major crude oil port forced Chinese Petroleum on Monday to sharply reduce production at its only northern Taiwan refinery, executives said.

The total shutdown of the state-run firm's crude offloading unit at Taoyuan near Taiwan's main international airport was the second in less than three weeks and threatened production of the refinery's main product -- aircraft fuel.
Any protracted delay was expected to have repercussions through the Taoyuan refinery's crude supply system.
Already one tanker was held up at the oil port, awaiting repairs that would allow it to unload its 300,000-tonne shipment of African crude, Chinese Petroleum officials confirmed.
At peak operation the plant processes 200,000 barrels or roughly 27,000 tonnes of crude oil per day. It represents about 28 percent of the island's total refining capacity of 720,000 barrels per day.
Chinese Petroleum officials met on Monday morning to discuss emergency contingencies for purchases of alternative supplies of the jet fuel for Taiwan's civilian and military airports.
Chinese Petroleum operates two other refineries in southern Taiwan but neither makes jet fuel.
Shutdowns of the refinery in earlier years have forced airlines operating in Taiwan to scramble for jet fuel in Hong Kong, Japan and Singapore, Chinese Petroleum officials said.

The oil company said it had enough crude in storage to run the Taoyuan refinery for at least 10 days, and spokesman Fang Yi-shan said engineers were confident the repairs could be completed in that time.

However, sources at the Taoyuan refinery were cautious about Fang's prediction, noting supertyphoon Violet was nearing Taiwan and could complicate, slow or even halt the repairs even if it does not make landfall.

Forecasters said Violet, packing 150 mile per hour winds, could pass northeast of Taiwan, but refinery officials said it was still expected to create dangerously high tides and powerful currents at Taoyuan.
Fang and other executives blamed the port shutdown on pipeline problems, but declined to give details.
A refinery official said the company shut one of the facility's two primary processing units. The move reduced production to 34 percent of capacity.
"The reduction will allow the refinery to maintain operations with the limited supplies of crude on hand," the official said.
Officials declined to say whether the decision meant engineers feared repairs to the pipeline could take longer than 10 days.
Officials would make no prediction as to when the stalled tanker, identified as the Vanadas, would be able to unload its cargo.
Details about the tanker and the specific source of its crude, identified only as African, were not immediately available.

Chinese Petroleum would not say whether there was any link between the Taoyuan oil port's new problems and a similar total shutdown on August 29, when crude was found to be leaking from the twin-unit offshore platform during offloading of a tanker.
